justification_text:
The point estimates at each time horizon were likely driven by a stable baseline assumption that aligns with recent observable trends or averages in the underlying data. The use of the same point estimate across all horizons (131.59) suggests an expectation that, in the absence of dramatic new information or shocks, the central value will remain steady over time. This could imply that there is limited directional bias in the data you're forecasting, or that historical movement has tended to mean-revert around similar levels.

The growing width of the confidence intervals as the forecast horizon extends reflects the increasing uncertainty inherent in predicting further into the future. In the short term (1-day horizon), the model may be relying on recent data or patterns, which generally reduces uncertainty and keeps the range tighter. However, over a week or a month, more variables and potential unknowns come into play. These sources of uncertainty might include market volatility, broader economic trends, new information entering the system, or random noise that becomes increasingly impactful over time.

Certain risks or events could cause outcomes to fall outside the confidence intervals, particularly over longer horizons. For instance, unexpected events like major geopolitical developments, policy changes, regulatory shifts, or sudden market disruptions could create larger-than-anticipated deviations. Similarly, if the underlying assumptions of the model don't capture a key driver of variation—such as a trend that accelerates or reverses direction—forecast accuracy may falter. In a month-long horizon, such risks become even more pronounced, as there is more time for unforeseen factors to emerge and compound their effects.
